midi_in.what: Your keyboard, as signals. Every key you play becomes a voice, and each voice gets its own pitch, gate, velocity and pressure.
midi_in.does: When you press a key it gives the note a free voice and sets that voice's PITCH to the note and GATE to 1; when you let go, GATE falls to 0. VELOCITY holds how hard you played. The mod wheel and pitch bend are shared by all voices.
midi_in.why: A modular synth does nothing by itself: something has to say which note and when. MIDI In turns your playing into the pitch and gate signals the rest of the patch follows.
midi_in.where: At the start of almost every patch: PITCH into the oscillators (and a filter's KEY), GATE into the envelopes. One MIDI In is enough; its outputs can feed as many inputs as you like.
try: Plug VELOCITY into a VCA's CV (through a Mixer with the envelope) so harder notes are louder.
Plug MOD WHEEL into a filter's CUTOFF and play with the wheel.

bend_range.what: How far the pitch bend wheel bends the notes, in semitones (0 to 12).
bend_range.does: The wheel's -1..+1 is scaled by this and added to PITCH, so everything following PITCH bends together.
bend_range.why: 2 semitones is the usual range for expressive bends; 12 gives octave dives and swoops; 0 leaves the wheel free to use only through the BEND output.
try: Set it to 7 and bend up a fifth at the end of a phrase.

pitch.what: The note of each voice, 1 per octave (0 is middle C), with the pitch bend added.
pitch.does: It jumps to the new note when a key is pressed and stays there after you let go, so the release of a note keeps its pitch.
pitch.why: This is what makes the oscillators play the notes you press. Without it every key would play the same pitch.
pitch.where: Into each oscillator's PITCH; into a filter's KEY so bright notes stay bright; through a Slew first for glide; into a Sequencer's TRANSPOSE to play a pattern from a key.

gate.what: 1 while a key is held, 0 when it's let go: one gate per voice.
gate.does: It rises the moment you press and falls the moment you let go. With one voice, playing legato (pressing a new key before letting go of the last) keeps it at 1.
gate.why: It is the timing of your playing. Envelopes need it to know when to start (attack) and when to let go (release).
gate.where: Into an envelope's GATE (usually); into a VCA's CV for a plain on/off; into an LFO's RESET so each note's wobble starts the same way.

velocity.what: How hard the key was struck, 0 (softest) to 1 (hardest), held for the whole note.
velocity.why: Dynamics: a synth that answers to how you play sounds more alive. Classic synths often ignored it; here you choose what it moves.
velocity.where: Into a filter's CUTOFF (harder is brighter), or mixed with the envelope into a VCA's CV (harder is louder), or an envelope's level through a VCA.

pressure.what: Aftertouch: how hard you press into a key you're already holding, 0..1. Not every keyboard sends it.
pressure.why: It lets you change a note while it sounds, with the same hand that plays it: swell the vibrato or open the filter by leaning on the key.
pressure.where: Into an oscillator's FM through a VCA opened by an LFO (vibrato on pressure), or a filter's CUTOFF.

mod_wheel.what: The modulation wheel on your keyboard, 0..1, the same for every voice.
mod_wheel.why: A hand control for anything: the usual job is bringing in vibrato, but it can open a filter, speed up an LFO or bring in an effect.
mod_wheel.where: Into a VCA's CV with an LFO going through the VCA, then on to an oscillator's FM: the wheel sets how much vibrato.
try: Plug it straight into a filter's CUTOFF with CV turned up, and play the wheel like a wah pedal.

bend.what: The pitch bend wheel, -1 (down) to +1 (up), 0 at rest, the same for every voice.
bend.why: PITCH already includes the bend; this output lets you bend something else: the filter, an LFO's rate, the pulse width.
bend.where: Into a filter's CUTOFF for a wheel-controlled sweep, or an LFO's RATE.

oscillator.what: The source of the tone: it makes a steady, repeating wave at the pitch you give it. Four waves come out at once: saw, pulse, triangle and sine.
oscillator.does: PITCH sets how many times a second the wave repeats (440 times a second is the A above middle C). OCTAVE and TUNE shift that. Each output is the same pitch with a different shape, and the shape decides the tone: how many harmonics (higher overtones) it has.
oscillator.why: Almost every synth sound starts with an oscillator. A filter can only take away what the oscillator gives it, so the wave you pick is the raw material of the sound.
oscillator.where: PITCH from MIDI In (or a sequencer); an output into a filter, a mixer or straight into a VCA; the VCA then goes to the Output. Two oscillators into a Mixer make a thicker sound.
try: Listen to each output in turn on the same note.
Right-click each output to see its shape on the scope.
Add a second oscillator a few cents off for a thicker sound (lesson 6).

octave.what: Shifts the pitch by whole octaves, -3 to +3.
octave.does: Each step doubles or halves the frequency; the note name stays the same.
octave.why: Put a bass where a bass belongs (-1, -2) without playing at the bottom of the keyboard, or stack a second oscillator an octave above or below for weight.

tune.what: Shifts the pitch up or down by up to 12 semitones, smoothly.
tune.does: Small amounts (0.05 to 0.2 semitones) detune; whole numbers transpose: 7 is a fifth, 12 an octave.
tune.why: Two oscillators slightly apart drift in and out of phase, which sounds wide and rich (the 'beating' you hear). A second oscillator at +7 plays a fifth: a power chord from one key.
try: With two oscillators on the same note, turn one's TUNE slowly from 0: hear the beating start slow and speed up.

width.what: The pulse wave's width: how much of each cycle it's up rather than down (5% to 95%).
width.does: At 50% it's a square: hollow, woody, with only odd harmonics. Narrower (or wider) gets thinner and more nasal, down to a reedy buzz.
width.why: It changes the tone of the PULSE output without a filter. Moving it over time (PWM) is one of the classic synth sounds.

fm_amount.what: How far the FM input moves the pitch, in octaves for a full-size signal.
fm_amount.does: An LFO's -1..+1 times this is added to the pitch: at 0.03 it's a gentle vibrato, at 1 a full octave up and down.
fm_amount.why: This is how the pitch moves on its own: vibrato from an LFO, a drop or rise at the start of each note from an envelope (great for drums and zaps).
try: An LFO at 5 Hz and FM at 0.02 to 0.05: vibrato.
An envelope with a short decay and FM at 2: a laser zap.

lin_fm_amount.what: How much the LIN FM input shakes the frequency itself.
lin_fm_amount.does: The input times this speeds the wave up and slows it down at audio rate. When the input is another oscillator, the result isn't a wobble but new tones, sideband frequencies around the note.
lin_fm_amount.why: This is FM synthesis: bells, electric piano, glass, metal, from just two sine waves. A little gives brightness; a lot gives clangs.
try: Another oscillator's SINE into LIN FM, an octave up. Turn this from 0: the tone gets brighter. Now tune the other one off whole octaves: bells and gongs (lesson 7).

pwm_amount.what: How far the PWM input moves the pulse width.
pwm_amount.does: The input times this is added to WIDTH (kept between 5% and 95%), so the PULSE output's tone changes with it.
pwm_amount.why: A pulse whose width slowly moves sounds like several oscillators chorusing together: rich, swirling strings and pads from one oscillator.
try: A slow LFO (0.5 Hz) into PWM, this at 0.3, listen to PULSE.

pitch.what: The note to play, 1 per octave, 0 is middle C.
pitch.does: Added to OCTAVE and TUNE: the oscillator plays exactly what comes in, so anything that changes this signal changes the note.
pitch.why: With nothing plugged in the oscillator just drones on middle C (plus OCTAVE and TUNE). Plugging in MIDI In's PITCH makes it play your keys.
pitch.where: From MIDI In's PITCH, a Sequencer's PITCH, or a Slew (for glide).

fm.what: Pitch modulation: a signal that moves the pitch, scaled by the FM knob.
fm.does: It's added to the pitch in octaves, so the same amount moves every note by the same musical interval.
fm.why: Vibrato, trills, sirens, pitch drops at the start of a note: anything where the pitch moves by itself.
fm.where: From an LFO (vibrato), an envelope (pitch sweeps), a Sample & Hold (random notes).

lin_fm.what: Linear frequency modulation, scaled by LIN FM: another audio signal shaking this oscillator's frequency.
lin_fm.does: Unlike FM, which moves the pitch musically, this pushes the frequency directly and evenly, so a fast signal here creates new frequencies rather than a wobble.
lin_fm.why: The way to get FM tones: bells, metal, glassy keys.
lin_fm.where: From another oscillator (usually its SINE). An envelope through a VCA on the way in makes the brightness fade like a struck bell.

pwm.what: Pulse-width modulation, scaled by PWM: a signal that moves the pulse width.
pwm.why: To make the PULSE output's tone move on its own: a swirling, chorused sound.
pwm.where: From a slow LFO, or an envelope for a tone that changes as the note goes.

sync.what: Hard sync: another signal resets this oscillator's wave each time it rises through zero.
sync.does: This oscillator is forced to restart at the other's rate, so its pitch is locked to the other one. Tuning this one higher no longer changes the note: it changes the tone, with a tearing, vocal sound.
sync.why: Sync gives aggressive leads that cut through. Sweeping this oscillator's pitch (FM from an envelope) while it's synced is the classic screaming lead.
sync.where: From another oscillator's SAW or SINE, both playing the same PITCH.
try: Sync this to another oscillator, then turn this one's TUNE up slowly: the pitch stays, the tone tears (lesson 6).

saw.what: The sawtooth wave: a ramp up and a drop, every cycle.
saw.does: It has every harmonic, each a little quieter than the one before: the brightest, buzziest wave here.
saw.why: With so much in it, a filter has plenty to shape: the go-to wave for basses, brass, strings and leads.
try: Right-click it to see the ramp on the scope.

pulse.what: The pulse wave: up for part of each cycle, down for the rest. At 50% WIDTH it's a square.
pulse.does: A square has only the odd harmonics: hollow, woody, like a clarinet. Narrow widths sound thinner and nastier.
pulse.why: A different colour from the saw, and the one wave whose tone you can move without a filter (WIDTH and PWM).

triangle.what: The triangle wave: up and down in straight lines.
triangle.does: Like the square, only odd harmonics, but they fall away much faster: soft and round, a little like a flute or an ocarina.
triangle.why: For gentle sounds that don't need a filter, and as a smooth sub under another wave.

sine.what: The sine wave: the pure note, with no harmonics at all.
sine.does: A filter can't change it (there's nothing above the note to take away), so it stays the same through one.
sine.why: A clean sub-bass under a busier sound, a soft whistle, and the best modulator for FM: its sideband tones are clean.

noise.what: A source of random signal: hiss, with no pitch.
noise.does: Each sample is random. WHITE has all frequencies equally (bright, like steam); PINK has less treble and more weight, like rain or the sea.
noise.why: Noise is the raw material for anything without a clear pitch: snares, hi-hats, wind, breath, the hiss of a wave. Into a Sample & Hold it gives random steps; through a slow filter it's random modulation.
noise.where: Into a filter (a band-pass for a snare, a high-pass for hats), then a VCA opened by a short envelope. Or into a Mixer with an oscillator to add breath.
try: WHITE into a State-Variable Filter's IN, listen to BAND, sweep CUTOFF: whooshing wind (lesson 9 builds drums like this).

white.what: White noise: every frequency at equal strength.
white.why: The brightest hiss: filtered, it becomes hi-hats, snares, cymbal-like washes and sweeps.

pink.what: Pink noise: each octave as loud as the next, so it has less treble than white.
pink.why: A softer, more natural hiss for wind, surf and rain, and smoother random modulation.

output.what: Where the sound leaves Konnekt for your speakers or headphones.
output.does: Everything plugged into LEFT and RIGHT is turned up or down by VOLUME and sent out. All the voices are mixed together here.
output.why: Nothing is heard until something is plugged into it: it's the end of every patch.
output.where: At the end: from a VCA (so notes start and stop), or from an effect's LEFT and RIGHT outputs.
try: If nothing sounds, right-click the outputs along your chain, working back from here, and see where the signal stops.

volume.what: The overall volume of the patch.
volume.why: Several voices add up and some patches are much louder than others: keep it where your speakers are comfortable. The meter at the top right shows the level.

left.what: The left speaker. If RIGHT is empty, it goes to both.
left.why: A mono patch only needs this one cable.

right.why: For stereo: an effect's RIGHT output, or a second voice panned apart. Empty, the right speaker plays LEFT.

scope.what: A screen on the rack that draws a signal as it happens: time across, value up and down.
scope.does: It shows whatever is plugged into IN, and passes it through THRU unchanged so you can put it in the middle of a cable. Click its screen to show it there.
scope.why: Seeing a signal makes it make sense: the shape of a wave, an envelope rising and falling, an LFO, what a filter does to a saw.
scope.where: Anywhere you want to look: between an oscillator and a filter, after the filter (watch the corners round off as you lower CUTOFF), on an envelope.
try: Put it after a filter, play a saw and turn CUTOFF down: watch the sharp edges soften.

time.what: How much time the screen shows across: 5, 20 or 80 milliseconds.
time.why: 5 ms shows the shape of a single wave in detail; 80 ms shows slower movement like a fast envelope or a vibrato.

in.what: What to look at: any signal.
in.why: Audio, an envelope, an LFO: anything you plug in is drawn.

thru.what: What comes in, passed on unchanged.
thru.why: So you can watch a signal on its way somewhere instead of taking it off its path.
